what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a new way of representing a 3D scene as thousands of fuzzy ellipsoids; a SLAM system (Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping) uses it to build a map and track a camera's position in real time. The problem is that even the fastest existing 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at only 0.8-14 frames per second on a modern edge GPU — far below the 30 fps needed for live AR/VR or robotics. RTGS combines software pruning and downsampling tricks with a custom hardware chip that plugs into the GPU, achieving real-time 30+ fps with up to 82x better energy efficiency.
method_in_detail:
The problem. Rendering and gradient (error-signal) computation together consume over 80% of the pipeline's time. Two root causes: (1) most of the thousands of ellipsoids barely matter for the current camera pose, yet still get drawn; (2) pixels vary wildly in how many ellipsoids overlap them, causing some GPU threads to sit idle while others are buried.

Software fix 1: Adaptive Gaussian pruning. Each training iteration already computes a gradient for every ellipsoid — a measure of how much moving that ellipsoid would change the image error. RTGS reuses those gradients as importance scores, progressively masking and then permanently deleting low-importance ellipsoids across iterations. Because the gradients were already being computed, this adds zero extra work for importance evaluation.

Software fix 2: Dynamic downsampling. Consecutive non-keyframes (frames that are not used to update the map) look almost identical to each other. The system processes the frame immediately after a keyframe at only 1/16 of full resolution; resolution ramps back up gradually as the camera moves further from the keyframe, reaching at most 1/4 resolution. The keyframe-identification step is reused to trigger this scaling with no added overhead.

Hardware fix 1: Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU). The unit records which pixels finished quickly (light workload) and which finished slowly (heavy workload) in iteration N, then pairs one heavy pixel with one light pixel in iteration N+1 to share a compute unit — exploiting the observation that workload patterns barely change between adjacent iterations. A streaming strategy also lets compute units grab the next patch of pixels as soon as they free up, rather than waiting for a global sync.

Hardware fix 2: Rendering and Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer. The backward pass recomputes a value called transmittance (how much light passes through each ellipsoid) that was already computed — and then discarded — in the forward pass. The R&B Buffer stores those intermediate values from the forward pass in a small on-chip buffer, cutting the backward-pass latency for the critical alpha-gradient step from 20 cycles to 4 cycles.

Hardware fix 3: Gradient Merging Unit (GMU). Multiple pixels touching the same ellipsoid try to update its gradient simultaneously, forcing serialised 'atomic add' operations (like a traffic light at a merge). The GMU uses a Benes network — a rearrangeable switch fabric — to sort incoming gradients by ellipsoid ID, then reduces them in a pipelined tree of adders, eliminating the collisions. Gradient merging latency drops 68%.

The result. Implemented in 28 nm at 500 MHz (8.1 W, 28 mm²), RTGS achieves 30+ fps on all four tested indoor datasets across three different SLAM algorithms, versus 0.8-14 fps on the same edge GPU alone, with up to 48.8x speedup and 82.5x better energy efficiency.
what_it_does_plain: RTGS makes real-time 3D scene mapping possible on low-power edge devices — robots, AR headsets — by combining smart software (skip unimportant ellipsoids, process non-key frames at lower resolution) with a dedicated add-on chip that fixes the GPU's three biggest inefficiencies: unbalanced pixel workloads, redundant recomputation, and serialised gradient updates.
